I can't tell whether your boat is recalled yet, because I need its model, year, or hull ID number (HIN). I did find a few Bayliner recalls in the Coast Guard's public recall database.

**Bayliner recalls I found:**

| Recall # | Model | Date opened |
|---|---|---|
| 23CG0010 | Bayliner Element M15 | 2023-06-23 |
| 100012S | Bayliner 195BR, 215BR, 197SD | 2010-05-18 |
| 080028T | Bayliner 205NBR | 2008-06-20 |

Four other recalls were filed by Brunswick Family Boat Co. (manufacturer code BLB), the company that makes Bayliner boats:

This list isn't complete. The page I read was truncated, and older recalls may be missing. Engine and component recalls are also listed under the parts maker, such as Mercury, Volvo Penta, or Dometic. If your boat has one of those parts, it could be recalled even though Bayliner isn't named.

**To check your boat:**
1. **Coast Guard database:** Go to https://www.uscgboating.org/content/recalls.php. You can search by manufacturer code (BLB for Bayliner), model, and year.
2. **Your HIN:** It's a 12-character code on the starboard side of the transom, near the top. Each recall page lists the affected HIN ranges.
3. **Bayliner or Brunswick:** Give your HIN to a Bayliner dealer or to Brunswick customer service. They can look up open recalls for your specific boat, including ones that don't appear in public lists.
4. **Engine:** Check the engine brand and serial number against the manufacturer's recall page (Mercury, Yamaha, Volvo Penta, and so on).

If you tell me the model, year, and engine, I can check which of these recalls apply and read the details of any that match.

finalAnswer:
I couldn't find a Coast Guard proposed rule on towing vessel inspections, so I can't give you a comment deadline. I searched the Federal Register for Coast Guard documents on towing vessels, towing vessel inspection and Subchapter M, which is the inspection regulation for towing vessels. None of the results was a proposed rule on that topic.

The closest matches were not about towing vessel inspections:
- **Request for Information on Multi-Service Vessels and Vessels of Opportunity:** published 2025-10-02, with comments closing 2025-12-01. It's a notice, not a proposed rule, and it covers different vessels.
- **Other proposed rules that mention towing vessels in passing:**
  - Cybersecurity in the Marine Transportation System. Its comment period closed 2024-04-22.
  - Lifejacket Approval Harmonization. Its comment period closed 2023-06-06.
  - Mariner Credentialing Program Transformation. Its comment period closed 2024-05-13.

If you can tell me more, I can look again. A Federal Register document number or title, or the rough publication date, would help. If the rule is very recent, it may also not be indexed yet. Regulations.gov lists the docket and its current deadline.

finalAnswer:
Yes. NAVAREA IX, coordinated by Pakistan, covers the Red Sea, and it has an active piracy warning for the Bab al-Mandab area. I pulled this from the Pakistan Hydrographic Office's NAVAREA IX page, which was current as of 9 Oct 2026.

**Active Red Sea warnings, most urgent first**

| Warning | Issued | Area | Subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| **363/26** | 07 Oct 2026, 1900 UTC | Bab al-Mandab Strait | **Piracy activity** reported at 12-58.00N 043-12.00E. Mariners are told to keep clear and use extreme caution. The warning self-cancels at 142359 UTC Oct 26. It also cancels NAVAREA IX 361/26. |
| 286/26 | 17 Aug 2026 | Saudi Arabia, Jeddah Islamic Port | Restricted area established. |
| 254/26 | 23 Jul 2026 | Saudi Arabia, Yanbu Commercial Port | Dredging operation. |

Older Red Sea warnings from 2024–2025 also appear on the "in force" list (350/26). They include 339/25 (MV Eternity C reported sunk), 328/25 (risk of explosion off Yemen) and several missing or unlit buoys off Saudi Arabia. I did not open those texts, so check the full messages if you need details.

**Other notes**
- NAVAREA IX also has current warnings for the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. These include an oil tanker, LIPSI, reported in a security incident and drifting near the Strait of Hormuz (352/26). They are outside the Red Sea, so I haven't listed them in full.
- The northern Red Sea, such as the Gulf of Suez and Egyptian waters, may also be covered by coastal or NAVAREA III warnings. I didn't check those.
- Web copies of warnings are informational only. For navigation, use the official broadcasts (Inmarsat-C SafetyNET, Iridium SafetyCast, NAVTEX).

You can read the full text of 363/26 here: https://hydrography.paknavy.gov.pk/wp-content/plugins/navarea-warnings/custom_uploaded_warnings_for_navarea/20261007SEC%20363.txt

*   [NAVAREA IX WARNINGS](https://hydrography.paknavy.gov.pk/navarea-ix-warnings/)

Hydrographer of Pakistan (HoP) leads both HQ NAVAREA IX and National Coordinator setup for the purpose of transmission of navigational warnings. These warnings are issued in accordance with IMO resolution A.706(17) as amended to fulfill provisions of SOLAS Chapter V. It may be noted that these warnings are normally based on information provided/ received through various sources that may not be complete or reliable all the time; therefore mariners are requested to be vigilant and careful while taking decisions thereof.

Further, this website though regularly updated/ monitored, however availability of Navigational Warnings on the web does not relieve Masters/ Captains of the requirement to receive Navigational Warnings via IMO/ IHO approved broadcast systems.

finalAnswer:
I couldn't get a reliable live figure. The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) publishes the real-time numbers, but they sit in an interactive dashboard that my tools couldn't read.

- **Official ACP dashboard:** The "Vessels Waiting to Transit the Panama Canal" page showed it was last updated on 9 Oct 2026 at 7:18 AM. The queue counts and the 28-day average waiting-time chart are graphics, so no numbers came through.
- **ShipNext:** It lists an average waiting time of about 5.4 days for the Panama Canal. It labels this "Month" and doesn't say which ship types or which dates it covers.
- **MasOceans:** Its page gives a 10-day estimate (North / South), but it is clearly outdated, with forecast files dated "Aug 31". I wouldn't rely on it.

| Vessel size | North | South |
|---|---|---|
| NeoPanamax | 0.5–2 days | 0.5–2 days |
| Super | 3–6 days | 1–4 days |
| Regular | 0.5–1 day | 0.5–2 days |

The ACP's waiting figures cover only vessels without a booking. Ships with a confirmed reservation transit on their booked date, so they mostly avoid the wait. Non-booked ships are the ones that can queue for days.

For the exact current number, open the ACP dashboard directly: [Vessels waiting to transit](https://apps.pancanal.com/t/TI/views/DashboardWaitingtoTransit/DashboardWaitingtoTransit-EN). The ACP's [Vessel ETA and Transit Booking page](https://pancanal.com/en/maritime-services/vessel-eta-and-transit-booking/) also links to the booking-slot availability pages.

Location: The Panama Canal crosses the isthmus of Panama from NW to SE. General overview: The length of the canal is approx 82km (51nm) from deep water in the Caribbean to deep water in the Pacific. It is located in the territory of the Republic of Panama. The Panama Canal Authority is responsible for the operation of the Panama Canal. In fulfilling its obligation, the Authority manages, operates and maintains the Canal, its complementary works, installations and equipment and provides for the orderly transit of vessels through the canal. Traffic figures: Approx 12,500 transits of vessels, 204,500,000t of cargo transit through the Canal annually. Load line zone: Tropical. Max size: Current Max Dimensions: Largest vessel handled: Panamax: LOA 299m, beam 32.6m. Maximum Length: The maximum acceptable LOA for a regular transit of a commercial vessel, including the bulbous bow, is 289.5m (950ft). For passenger and container ships, the max LOA may be up to 294.1m (965ft). Advance approval is required for the initial transit of all vessels which exceed 274.3m (900ft). The max acceptable LOA for a regular transit of an integrated tug-barge combination is 274.3m (900ft), including the length of the tug. A tug-barge combination must transit together as one unit, with the tug supplying the propelling power. The max acceptable aggregate LOA for a transit of a non-self-propelled vessel is 259m (850ft), including the length of accompanying tugs. Accompanying tugs must lock through with the non self propelled vessel. Max Beam: The max acceptable extreme beam for a regular transit of a commercial vessel or of an integrated tug-barge is 32.3m (106ft). Max Height: The max allowable height for any vessel transiting the Canal or entering the port of Balboa at any state of the tide is 57.9m (190ft) measured from the waterline to its highest point. No. As of the FAA's TFR list (data as of Fri, Oct 9, 2026, 12:43 UTC), I found no active TFR over Cape Canaveral or Brevard County.

- **No space operations TFRs.** Launch TFRs are listed under the "SPACE OPERATIONS" type, and none of the 92 current records has that type.
- **Closest Florida TFRs are all well away from the Cape:**
  - Palm Coast (HAZARDS, 6/8591), today, about 90 nm north.
  - Daytona Beach (UAS public gathering, 6/8298), Oct 14–18, about 50 nm north.
  - Jacksonville (air show, 6/8389), Oct 15–18.
  - Mayport (SECURITY, 6/7134), through Oct 10.
  - Tampa (UAS public gathering, 6/7170), Oct 9–10.
  - Key West and Palm Beach security TFRs.
- **Standing restrictions still apply.** The nationwide security TFRs, such as the stadium and Disney World ones, aren't specific to the Cape. The restricted and warning airspace around the Cape and Kennedy Space Center isn't a TFR and won't appear on this list.

I only checked the FAA TFR list. TFRs for launches are often issued only a few days ahead, so a new one could be added later. Before you fly, get an official briefing from 1-800-WX-BRIEF, Leidos or ForeFlight and check NOTAMs at the time of your flight. I didn't check Cape-specific launch NOTAMs or the 45th Weather Squadron's launch schedule.
